performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: “Wenn dein Mütterlein” is the third of the Kindertotenlieder. In it a mother comes through the door, and the father looks down for the little face beside her. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings it with Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic, and the orchestra in this song has no violins.

sections.label: A · Cor anglais, bassoons, pizzicato cellos
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and bassoons above plucked cellos

sections.label: A′ · Opening returns, harp and pizzicato bass
sections.mNote: Harp and pizzicato double bass return to the opening material.

sections.label: Coda · Cor anglais, horns and cellos
sections.mNote: Horns and bowed cellos; ends in G major.

cues.title: Opening, cor anglais and bassoons
cues.text: Cor anglais and bassoons play above plucked cellos. Mahler marks the opening “Schwer, dumpf” — heavy, muffled. When Fischer-Dieskau enters, the orchestra has no violins, and they are left out for the whole song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), p. 33: instrumentation and opening marking; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rückert’s text, first stanza
cues.text: In Rückert’s poem the father turns towards his wife, then looks below her face, “näher nach der Schwelle” (nearer the threshold). That is where the daughter used to appear when she came in beside her mother.
cues.evidence: Rückert, Wenn dein Mütterlein, first stanza as set by Mahler; German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text. Our translation.

cues.title: Children’s-song melody and accompaniment
cues.text: The voice line follows the pattern of a children’s song, and at times of a chanted counting rhyme. Beneath it the orchestra plays linear parts at twice the speed of the voice. These parts recall the first song.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), on song 3: children’s-song melodies, counting rhymes, and a linear accompaniment moving twice as fast as the voice and recalling the first song: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Second stanza, rehearsal 3
cues.text: The cor anglais begins again, now over harp and pizzicato double bass. In the second stanza the mother carries a candle, and the child is pictured entering the room behind her. In Fischer-Dieskau’s closing lament, she is called a light extinguished too soon.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 40–46, rehearsal 3 onwards; Rückert’s second stanza. The changed bass scoring is discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Venues and string section, 1905
cues.text: Mahler preferred small rooms for these songs. In 1905 he chose the Kleiner Musikvereinssaal for the Vienna performances and then the Stephaniesaal in Graz. His string section had about ten first violins at most, and this song has no violins.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder, scoring note: good evidence that the small venues were the composer’s own choice and that the strings were probably no more than 10, 8, 6, 6 and 4 (citing Hefling and Hilmar-Voit). Performances: Vienna 29 January and 3 February 1905, Graz 1 June 1905: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: Alma Mahler on the Kindertotenlieder
cues.text: Alma Mahler could not understand how her husband could bewail the deaths of children within an hour of kissing his own, who were “in the best of health and spirits”. She exclaimed: “For Heaven’s sake, don’t tempt Providence!” Mahler completed the cycle in the summer of 1904.
cues.evidence: Alma Mahler, Gustav Mahler: Memories and Letters, as quoted by Georg Predota, Interlude, 29 January 2019: https://interlude.hk/mahler-kindertotenlieder-premiered-today-1905/. The exclamation is also given in Michael Kennedy, Mahler (Master Musicians), Edward Seckerson, Mahler: His Life and Times (1982), and Stephen Johnson, Mahler (2007) (full-text excerpts seen); the memoir itself was not opened. Kubik dates songs 2 and 5 to 1904: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Return of the opening, closing bars
cues.text: After the voice has finished, the cor anglais repeats the opening. The cellos now play arco, with the horns close beside them. The song ends on a G major chord, the dominant of C minor.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 47: Wieder wie zu Anfang, bowed cellos, horns and the final dominant chord. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: End of first stanza into reprise
transitions.from: A · Cor anglais, bassoons, pizzicato cellos
transitions.to: A′ · Opening returns, harp and pizzicato bass
transitions.how: The first stanza descends to its low “Töchterlein” and closes in C minor. After the ritardando, Wie zu Anfang restores the opening tempo and the cor anglais tune. Harp and plucked double bass replace the cello pulse. The bass clarinet holds one note across the join.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 40, rehearsal 3; Woltjer, song III, bars 31–33. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html

transitions.title: Bowed cellos replace the plucked pulse
transitions.from: A′ · Opening returns, harp and pizzicato bass
transitions.to: Coda · Cor anglais, horns and cellos
transitions.how: At Wieder wie zu Anfang the cor anglais returns, with horns and bowed cellos beneath it. The wind phrases lengthen and slow. Harp and low strings support the final chord, G major, the dominant of C minor, held under fermatas.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 47. The dominant ending is discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song III, printed pp. 33–47: cor anglais and plucked cellos at the opening, harp and double basses in the second stanza. Violins are silent throughout.

timeline.note: Opening: cor anglais and bassoon lines above the pizzicato cello pulse.
The baritone enters with the cor anglais and bassoons over pizzicato cellos.
Harp and plucked double basses replace the cellos beneath the returning cor anglais phrase.
Cor anglais, horns and bowed cellos recall the opening before the final G-major chord.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
